facts.text: This Hong Kong-American co-production cost about $250,000 and grossed $4.66 million in the US and Canada, plus 395,013 tickets in France alone.
Goof alert: in this opening dojo scene, the American flag on the wall is hung backward.
Screenwriter Keith W. Strandberg says his first draft, then titled Ring of Truth, ran roughly 200 pages. He learned on set to just write fights as 'they fight.'
Jean-Claude Van Damme was picked from a line of fighters at an open call. Screenwriter Keith W. Strandberg helped choose him over another guy who 'couldn't really move.'
Jean-Claude Van Damme's flying kick off a downed thug's shoulder was meant to hit Timothy D. Baker's chest. Baker says Van Damme kept hitting his face, knee and throat instead.
Van Damme's leap-off-a-crouching-man flying side kick returns in Bloodsport (1988), where the crouching man is the referee. Same stunt, same opening-move surprise.
This was director Corey Yuen's English-language debut. As a kid he had played an uncredited Japanese fighter in Bruce Lee's Fist of Fury (1972).
Though the story moves to Seattle, the film was shot mostly in Los Angeles, with only some exterior location work in Seattle itself.
Goof alert: Jason hangs his punching bag from a garage beam, but the bag jumps between shoulder height and head height from shot to shot.
No Retreat, No Surrender opened May 2, 1986 at number eleven at the US box office, earning $739,723 in its first week.
J.W. Fails (R.J. Madison) lied to the filmmakers that he could break dance and skateboard to land the role. A double did his dancing and skating.
Kurt McKinney (Jason) found the audition in the Drama-Logue paper. The lead was the only role left when he arrived, and he was cast right after reading.
Kurt McKinney's LAPD application was accepted the same day he won the lead. He passed on becoming a cop to act instead.
Why does bully Scott hate R.J.? A cafeteria scene where R.J. (J.W. Fails) trips Scott and spills his food was scripted to explain it, but it was never filmed.
Goof alert: this film is set in Seattle, but palm trees stand in the background of the burger-joint confrontation.
Producer Ng See-yuen came up with the idea of an American story with Hong Kong fighting. Strandberg says it had never been done before.
Actor Ryan Gosling has named No Retreat, No Surrender as one of his favorite films.
Screenwriter Keith W. Strandberg got past Hong Kong producer Ng See-yuen's gatekeepers by switching from English to Mandarin mid-call after other studios ignored him.
The Seattle dojo was a converted Van Nuys bowling alley. The dark arrows and dots on the wood floor are leftover bowling-lane markings.
Time Out compared the film to The Last Dragon, The Karate Kid and Rocky IV, saying it 'borrows heavily' and makes them look like masterpieces.
Jason Stillwell was written as a teenager, but Kurt McKinney was already 22 when filming began.
The film reached US theaters May 2, 1986, less than two months before The Karate Kid Part II. Reviewers constantly compared it to the first Karate Kid.
The pinball machine in the bar's background is Bally's 1982 Vector. The beer foam in Jason's dad's glass also changes drastically between shots.
During filming Jean-Claude Van Damme's car was in such bad shape that he often asked cast members to push it to start the engine after the day's shoot.
Patrick Goldstein of the Los Angeles Times called the film 'hilariously bad' and an 'amateurish clunker.' It has since built a cult following.
Goof alert: the red stain on Jason's shirt during the pool fight keeps changing in intensity from shot to shot.
Tae-jeong Kim, who plays Bruce Lee's ghost, was a real stand-in for Bruce Lee in Game of Death (1978) and Game of Death II (1980).
Goof alert: Jason's dad tears the Bruce Lee poster down, but half stays on the garage wall. Jason somehow arrives at the abandoned house holding the other half.
RiffTrax, with ex-MST3K stars Mike Nelson, Bill Corbett and Kevin Murphy, riffed this movie. It was also one of two films in the 2019 MST3K Live Great Cheesy Movie Tour.
Bruce Lee's ghost, Tae-jeong Kim, and Kurt McKinney spoke different languages in their scenes. They read cue cards and didn't know what the other said; Kim was dubbed later.
Goof alert: Jason greets Bruce Lee's ghost as 'Sensei Lee.' Lee was Chinese, so the proper title would be 'Sifu'; 'sensei' is Japanese.
A Korean dialogue coach wrote Korean lines timed to the English script for Tae-jeong Kim. Kurt McKinney reportedly called Kim only 'Sensei Lee' even off camera.
Screenwriter Keith W. Strandberg says he didn't want the Bruce Lee ghost to be exploitation. He saw it as a tribute to Bruce Lee, whose poster hung where he trained.
Kurt McKinney's two-finger push-ups were filmed with wires hoisting him up and down, hidden by the trees in the background.
Screenwriter Keith W. Strandberg says few US martial arts films existed in 1984, so the cast couldn't fight on camera. The crew taught them how to react and throw a pretty kick for the cameras.
Fight choreographer Hoi Mang doubled for both Kurt McKinney and Tae-jeong Kim in the back-somersault flip kick.
In the sandbag montage, Jason kicks a bag so hard it breaks. That wasn't planned.
The 2004 UK DVD uses a totally different score of stock music from Hong Kong films like Project A and My Lucky Stars, and a different theme song, 'Hold On To The Vision.'
Kurt McKinney didn't want to do the foot-in-a-looped-rope stunt, but director Corey Yuen insisted. It worked in the end.
Writer Keith W. Strandberg plays one of the thugs fighting Jason outside the bar. He says he turned the wrong way on a kick and never lived it down with the stuntmen.
While shooting the fight where Jason saves his father, Kurt McKinney accidentally kicked his opponent in the face with a flying kick.
British censors cut seven seconds from the cinema release: two shots of a Bruce Lee poster showing him holding nunchaku.
Some cuts include a Seattle Space Needle date for Jason (Kurt McKinney) and Kelly (Kathie Sileno) that is missing from other versions. Those versions trade it for other trims.
Two cuts exist: the international version and a US cut by New World Pictures that runs about 14 minutes shorter, with a different score and fewer comedic scenes.
The US version's theme is 'Hold On to the Vision,' sung by Kevin Chalfant. The UK cut was re-edited with a rock score and Joe Torono's 'Stand on Your Own.'
Goof alert: the 'MGM Grand Reno' tournament cuts big crowds and TV crews against fights that look like an empty gym with folding chairs.
Jean-Claude Van Damme is a supporting player here, but later video releases put him alone on the cover as the headline star.
Jean-Claude Van Damme inspired Mortal Kombat's Johnny Cage. The game was first planned as a Van Damme vehicle until Midway and Van Damme couldn't agree on a likeness fee.
Goof alert: the tournament crowd is completely silent in many shots of the fights.
Van Damme knocked stuntman Pete 'Sugarfoot' Cunningham out cold with a spinning kick, ran to help him, and ruined the take. On the retake he knocked him out again.
Goof alert: when Ivan kicks the referee out of the ring, the safety mattress the referee lands on is visible.
In 1993 Black Belt magazine ranked this film seventh on its list of top martial arts films for choreography, praising Van Damme's jump kicks.
Richard Scheib of Moria gave the film half a star and called it 'shabbily made.' He still called Jean-Claude Van Damme 'the one good performance' and praised his fight's 'physical poetry.'
Jean-Claude Van Damme originally had a two-picture deal with screenwriter Keith W. Strandberg but later broke the contract.
The movie got shout-outs in Pineapple Express (2008) and the video game Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon (2013). It also had a 1986 spoof, No Blood, No Surrender.
In the end credits, Jean-Claude Van Damme's character Ivan is listed as 'Karl Brezdin.'
It was a big hit on video, which led to sequels. In parts of Europe the film was released as Karate Tiger.
